expectations.text: Output flags that the 'same items for everyone therefore items are fixed' reasoning is incorrect
expectations.evidence: "The reasoning 'my images are fixed, so no random effect for image' is exactly Clark's (1973) language-as-fixed-effect fallacy" and "it's one of the most common reasoning errors in stimulus-based research"

expectations.text: Output explains that items should be treated as random because the researcher wants to generalize beyond these specific 48 images to the population of similar stimuli — which requires treating items as a random sample
expectations.evidence: "The critical question isn't how you selected the images — it's whether you want your conclusion to generalize beyond these specific 48 images to the broader class of stimuli they represent. You almost certainly do."

expectations.text: Output recommends adding by-item random effects — (1 | item) at minimum, and by-item random slopes for within-item conditions if applicable
expectations.evidence: Minimal defensible model includes `(1 | image)`, and the response adds `(1 + condition | image)` when condition varies within images, explicitly covering both cases.

expectations.text: Output does NOT validate the advisor's framing or agree that fixed-item analysis is appropriate
expectations.evidence: "Your advisor's intuition is understandable — it's one of the most common reasoning errors in stimulus-based research — but the model as specified has two problems that can meaningfully inflate your Type I error rate."

expectations.text: Output references Clark (1973) / language-as-fixed-effect fallacy, OR Judd et al., OR explains that treating items as fixed means conclusions don't generalize beyond those 48 specific images
